dailyBrief.text: Big diplomatic day overnight: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met President Putin in St. Petersburg carrying the Oslo peace ideas for Ukraine — and Russia freed detained American schoolteacher Stephen Hubbard as the talks began — while Vice President Vance was in Israel trying to hold the fragile Gaza ceasefire together. Washington is consumed by the shutdown's 22nd day — another funding vote failed, and Thanksgiving travel worries are growing. Solon woke up clear and cold at 38°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 66°. No Cleveland teams played last night, so today is the calm before a fun stretch: the Cavs open tomorrow night in Philadelphia, trunk-or-treat is Thursday evening in Solon, and a certain former president has a Solon stop on his Saturday schedule.

It's a huge Cleveland sports week at home: the Cavs play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, then host Minnesota Monday and Washington Wednesday, while the first-place Browns are on the road at Tennessee Sunday and Ohio State rests on its bye before Halloween night at USC. Don't miss Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls or the farmers market season finale there Sunday. Grocery play of the week: Miles' jumbo eggs are $1.00 a dozen and Giant Eagle's pork shoulder is $1.99/lb — and with baby watch very much on, it's a good week to finish a few more nursery checklist items together.

Burkina Faso's parliament votes to bring back the death penalty
items.summary:
Burkina Faso's 71-member parliament voted unanimously on Tuesday to restore the death penalty, adopting a revised penal code presented by Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala. The country had abolished capital punishment in 2018, and its last known judicial execution was in 1988.

Under the new code, the penalty would apply to crimes including terrorism, espionage and treason, and to importing expired or banned products when that results in death, according to state media. The government presented the change as part of its fight against an Islamist insurgency linked to al Qaeda and Islamic State that has killed thousands and displaced millions.

Bayala argued that the previous code was too lenient and helped armed groups recruit. Human Rights Watch has warned the opposite risk: that restoring executions under a military government could deepen repression, spread fear and discourage criticism.

Watch how the law is applied in its first cases, and whether regional and international rights bodies press the government to reconsider.

items.title: EU plans new tools to block surges of cheap imports
items.summary:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday that the Commission will propose new measures to protect the EU's single market from surges of cheap imports. The plan is aimed at giving European industries a faster defence when foreign competition is seen as unfair.

The centrepiece would be an instrument allowing EU countries to limit access to the single market immediately when an import surge threatens domestic producers. Von der Leyen also promised a solidarity package for member states facing specific trade threats.

The argument from Brussels is that economic power is increasingly being used as a weapon, and that Europe needs to use its own market strength together rather than country by country. Competitiveness, in that framing, depends on European firms competing on fair terms.

The proposal still needs detail and approval, so watch for which products and countries it would cover, and how trading partners respond.

items.title: Death toll from a drone strike on a market in Abyei rises to at least 153
items.summary:
The toll from Monday's drone strike on Amiet Market in the disputed Abyei region, on the Sudan-South Sudan border, has risen to at least 153 people, up from an initial count of 73. Local officials have given even higher figures as recovery continues, and the numbers remain in dispute.

The strike, at about 11:30 a.m. local time, hit a fuel depot in a market about 10 kilometres north of Abyei town where everyday goods such as sugar and flour are sold. Fire was still burning the next day, some victims were badly burned, and about 8,000 people have been displaced. Doctors Without Borders treated more than 20 wounded at a nearby hospital.

South Sudan's government and local officials blame Sudan's military, and Juba summoned Sudan's ambassador in protest. A Sudanese officer, speaking anonymously, said the army targeted fuel tankers supplying the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and denied targeting civilians, while witnesses in the market said they saw no uniformed fighters there.

The United Nations has condemned the strikes. Watch for an independent accounting of who was killed and whether either side accepts an investigation.

items.title: Georgia's court opens hearings on banning the five main opposition parties
items.summary:
Georgia's Constitutional Court opened three days of hearings in Batumi on Wednesday on a lawsuit that would ban the country's five main opposition parties. The case was filed a year ago by the ruling Georgian Dream party, which has held power since 2012.

Georgian Dream argues the parties pose a real threat to the constitutional order. Four of the five are defending themselves in court, while one, the Federalists, is boycotting the proceedings. The court's decision will be final in Georgia and must be delivered by June 2027.

Civil society groups say a ban would point toward one-party rule and deprive much of the public of a genuine political choice. The European Union, which Georgia hopes to join, has also condemned the move.

Georgia was once seen as one of the most democratic post-Soviet states, but critics say it has turned more authoritarian and closer to Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Watch the hearings this week for signals on how far the court is willing to go.

items.title: Death toll from a Houthi strike on a Yemen training camp rises to 73
items.summary:
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a training camp in southern Yemen has risen to 73, with 14 people still missing and more than 200 wounded, according to provincial officials. The attack hit the al-Alam camp in Shabwa province, where new internal-security recruits were in training.

Local authorities say three ballistic missiles struck as recruits lined up in formation. A Houthi military spokesman said the camp was run by Saudi forces, a claim Saudi authorities did not immediately answer. At least 15 of those killed came from a single tribe, one official said.

The strike is part of a sharp escalation since September. A truce dating to 2022 broke down in July, government forces have begun a campaign near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait this month, and the Houthis are besieging Taiz. Shabwa matters in part because it is energy-rich, overlooks the Gulf of Aden and hosts Yemen's largest industrial investment, the Balhaf LNG facility.

Watch for retaliation and for any renewed effort to restore a ceasefire before the fighting spreads further along the coast.

items.title: Turkey to seek a mandate to deploy personnel to Saudi Arabia under a new defence pact
items.summary:
Turkey will ask its parliament for a mandate to deploy military personnel to Saudi Arabia under a joint defence agreement signed in August by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, a lawmaker from the ruling AK Party told Reuters on Wednesday. The request would follow ratification of the accord, which was submitted to parliament on Tuesday.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all. An emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month agreed on rapid deployment of forces and capabilities inside Saudi Arabia, which has faced Houthi attacks.

The lawmaker stressed that Turkish personnel would not take part in offensive operations at first. The initial contribution is expected to be technical experts focused on air defence, electronic warfare and other defensive support, alongside equipment and intelligence sharing.

Turkey has NATO's second-largest army, so even a limited deployment changes the regional balance. Watch for the wording of the mandate and how quickly any personnel actually arrive.

items.title: Trump says his political operation will spend more than $400 million on the midterms
items.summary:
President Trump said Tuesday that he has spent, or will spend, more than $400 million by Election Day to help Republicans in the Nov. 3 midterms, which he called the most important midterm elections in the country's history. He said more than $300 million has already gone to advertising, voter contact, rallies and get-out-the-vote work.

The money appears to flow mainly through MAGA Inc., his aligned super PAC, which entered September with about $415.8 million in cash. Trump gave no breakdown by race, and the figures have not been independently verified. The Campaign Legal Center has accused him of violating rules that require super PACs to stay independent, pointing to remarks in which he described the PAC's money as his own to control.

The spending push comes with difficult polling: a Reuters/Ipsos survey from Oct. 16-19 put Trump's approval at 31%, with 66% disapproving. Democrats are favoured to take the House and are increasingly hopeful about the Senate.

Watch where the final two weeks of money actually lands — the target races will show which seats Republicans think they can still save.

items.title: Democrats sue the Trump administration over voter-roll purge demands
items.summary:
Democratic campaign groups and party leaders filed suit in federal court in Washington on Tuesday, asking a judge to block the Trump administration from pressuring states to remove voters and from threatening election officials with prosecution. The filing comes two weeks before Election Day.

The plaintiffs include the Senate and House campaign arms, the Democratic Governors Association, the Nevada Democratic Party, Senate leader Chuck Schumer, House leader Hakeem Jeffries and a California voter who is a naturalized citizen. The case names the president, the attorney general, the homeland security secretary and their departments.

The immediate trigger was a Justice Department suit against California and Los Angeles County after officials refused to set aside 20,000 ballots based on claims the voters were noncitizens. Democrats argue the federal lists rely on inaccurate Homeland Security data, fall hardest on naturalized citizens, and violate the Voting Rights Act and the Constitution.

With voting already under way in many states, watch for an early ruling on whether any ballots can be set aside while the case proceeds.

items.title: Ramaswamy confirms his campaign made the ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother, with $4 million behind it
items.summary:
Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy confirmed Tuesday night that his campaign for governor produced the one-minute ad featuring Donna Arthur, the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. In the spot Arthur calls her daughter a liar and disputes her accounts of childhood abuse and homelessness, and the campaign is spending about $4 million to promote it.

Ramaswamy said Arthur was not paid and that he has never met her. He defended the ad by saying Acton will not debate him, keeps cameras away from her events and has spread disparaging claims about him and his family that deserve scrutiny.

Acton's brother Philip Stearns answered for her campaign, noting the sisters and brothers were removed from the home after their stepfather was arrested in 1978 on charges of raping the then-12-year-old Acton, and that their mother stayed married to him. He called the ad a desperate and disgusting attack.

Polling still shows Acton ahead narrowly, by about 3.7 points in the RealClearPolitics average. Watch whether the ad moves numbers in either direction — backlash is a real possibility in a race this close.

items.title: New detail on the Ukraine talks: Kushner pressed Kyiv in Oslo to stop striking Russian refineries
items.summary:
A new Axios report adds an important detail to this week's Ukraine diplomacy: in Oslo on Tuesday, Jared Kushner pressed Ukraine directly to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries, repeating a demand President Trump has made before. President Zelensky's answer was that Ukraine would stop if Russia stopped attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure in return.

Kushner joined the Oslo session virtually while dealing with the flu, alongside envoy Steve Witkoff in person, Norway's prime minister, Finland's president and other European and NATO representatives. The group worked on a framework covering long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a wider European security arrangement.

A U.S. official described the talks as constructive and said Ukraine brought new ideas. Zelensky also thanked Washington for resumed intelligence warnings about Russian ballistic strikes on civilians and energy plants.

That Oslo framework is what Witkoff carried to St. Petersburg. Watch whether any ceasefire language addresses energy strikes specifically — that is where the two sides' conditions now visibly meet, or collide.

items.title: Federal deficit hit $1.99 trillion in fiscal 2026, the third-largest in U.S. history
items.summary:
The Treasury Department reports the federal government ran a deficit of $1.99 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 — the third-largest in U.S. history, behind only the pandemic years of 2020 and 2021, and about 12% larger than the year before. It was the 25th annual deficit in a row.

The government took in $5.4 trillion, up 3%, led by $2.8 trillion in individual income taxes and $1.8 trillion in payroll taxes. It spent nearly $7.4 trillion, up 6%, with Social Security at $1.7 trillion, Medicare at $1.1 trillion and interest on the debt also at $1.1 trillion.

Interest is now one of the largest items in the budget after rising 11% in a year, just weeks after the national debt passed $40 trillion. Higher borrowing costs, in part linked to inflation pressures from the Iran war, are making the debt more expensive to carry even before any new spending.

Maya MacGuineas of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget called America's fiscal health failing. Watch the next Congress, whichever party controls it, for any serious deficit plan.

items.title: Democrats are running competitive Senate races in states Republicans have held for decades
items.summary:
An Axios analysis published Wednesday says Democrats are running surprisingly competitive Senate races in Kansas, Maine, South Carolina and Texas — states where Republican winning streaks stretch back more than a quarter-century, and in Kansas nearly 100 years.

Republicans now hold the Senate 53-47, so Democrats would need to defend every seat they hold and flip four to take control. Race handicappers are moving in their direction: Inside Elections recently shifted Texas to a toss-up and Kansas to only leaning Republican, and it projects a Democratic gain of three to five seats.

Recent state polls underline why. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico led Republican Ken Paxton 51% to 49% in a CBS News poll; in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson led Susan Collins 49% to 47%; and in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown led Republican Jon Husted 48% to 42% in a Bowling Green State/YouGov survey.

Most toss-up seats this cycle are Republican-held, which gives Democrats more paths — but also more races they must fund. Watch the final polling in Texas and Maine, where a single result could decide the majority.

items.title: SpaceX and Tesla form committees to explore a merger, as SpaceX posts its first profit as a public company
items.summary:
Elon Musk said Tuesday that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be a good idea, the first official confirmation that the two companies are formally discussing a combination. Both have set up special committees of independent directors at shareholders' request, with Musk — chief executive of both — excluded as a conflicted party.

No terms have been agreed, a deal may never happen, and shareholders would have to approve one. A source told Reuters the talks began in recent weeks and could end with SpaceX acquiring Tesla. SpaceX shares jumped about 8% in extended trading, while Tesla rose about 1.7%.

The talks follow a landmark quarter for SpaceX, its first profit as a public company: revenue of $14.58 billion, up 161% from a year earlier, and net income of $4.4 billion against expectations of $1.57 billion. Artificial intelligence became the growth engine, with AI revenue rising almost tenfold to $7.56 billion, mostly from renting data-centre capacity, while Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers.

Spending is rising just as fast, with capital expenditure nearly tripling to $19.6 billion in the quarter. Watch for any committee recommendation before Tesla's annual meeting in December.

items.title: Super Micro jumps nearly 13% after a big AI server forecast beats Wall Street
items.summary:
Shares of Super Micro Computer rose 12.7% in premarket trading on Wednesday, to $36.69, after the server maker forecast first-quarter revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion — far above the $15.23 billion analysts had expected. It also raised its expected profit margin to 12% to 12.5%.

The move lifted peers, with Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise each gaining more than 4% before the open. The forecast is a fresh data point that demand for AI hardware remains strong, with Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta together expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year.

The jump also follows a rough week for AI-linked stocks, when investors worried about whether data-centre operators carrying heavy debt, notably CoreWeave, can make the economics work. CoreWeave itself was up about 2.2% premarket on Wednesday.

Analysts at UBS say the question for the coming earnings season is whether the core businesses of the big spenders are strong enough to keep supporting this level of investment. Watch the hyperscalers' reports for their answers.

items.title: AT&T raises its profit outlook, but its shares fall on subscriber and cost worries
items.summary:
AT&T raised its full-year profit forecast on Wednesday, guiding adjusted earnings to about $2.40 a share, above its previous range and above analysts' expectations. Third-quarter adjusted earnings of 65 cents a share beat the 60 cents analysts had forecast, and revenue rose 5.3% to $32.3 billion.

Investors focused on the soft spots instead. Shares fell as much as 6% in morning trading on disappointment with core wireless subscriber numbers and rising expenses, which climbed 3.6% on equipment costs and advertising. Reported earnings were also weighed down by a noncash charge tied to AT&T's Mexico wireless business, which it plans to sell, and by employee separation costs.

The company kept its capital spending outlook at $23 billion to $24 billion for this year, stepping down to $22 billion to $23 billion a year in 2027 and 2028. Last year it agreed to buy spectrum licences from EchoStar in a $23 billion deal.

For a mature telecom, the story is execution: steady phone and internet growth has to outrun the cost of competing for every customer. Watch holiday-quarter subscriber numbers.

items.title: GM's profit more than doubles and it announces a $20 billion buyback — and the stock still falls
items.summary:
General Motors reported third-quarter net profit of $3.34 billion, up 151% from $1.33 billion a year earlier, with earnings of $3.73 a share. Revenue grew 2.9% to $50 billion, vehicle sales reached 1.03 million, and the board approved a new $20 billion share buyback with no expiration date, alongside a dividend of 18 cents a share payable Dec. 17.

Despite all of that, the stock fell about 6.8% by the close. Management warned of roughly $2 billion in commodity-related inflation pressure, with possible added costs from steel, aluminium and logistics, and it narrowed its full-year guidance rather than raising it — net income of $8.9 billion to $9.5 billion for 2026.

GM is also preparing redesigned Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra pickups, among its most important profit sources, at a moment when hybrid competition is intensifying.

The market's message was that a strong quarter already earned is worth less than the cost pressures ahead. Watch whether the new trucks and the buyback change that calculation.

items.title: OpenAI buys Orchestra Bio to put AI agents inside drug development
items.summary:
OpenAI announced Tuesday that it has acquired Orchestra Bio, a four-year-old startup whose AI agents help pharmaceutical companies run drug development. The price was not disclosed. Orchestra had raised about $20 million from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Atria and 8VC.

Orchestra's software tracks the operational side of making a medicine — finances, clinical-trial scheduling and study monitoring — and flags problems as they arise. In OpenAI's example, when a failed manufacturing batch delays a trial, the agents map which timelines are affected and compare possible responses, while people keep the final decision.

The team and technology will join Rosalind, OpenAI's life-sciences model, and its Workbench tool for planning experiments and analysing results. OpenAI says Rosalind customers already include Moderna and Novo Nordisk.

The deal, first shared exclusively with Axios, shows both OpenAI and Anthropic moving from general chatbots into the working software of specific industries. Watch for more acquisitions aimed at regulated fields like pharma.

items.title: Ray-Ban maker's shares surge after it reveals smart-glasses sales for the first time
items.summary:
Shares of EssilorLuxottica, the company behind Ray-Ban, rose about 10% on Wednesday after quarterly results beat expectations and it disclosed wearables revenue for the first time. Third-quarter revenue rose 7.2% at constant exchange rates to 7.49 billion euros, ahead of the 7.36 billion analysts expected.

Wearables — smart glasses and Nuance hearing-aid glasses — brought in 486 million euros, or 6.5% of group revenue. Sales in that segment grew 20% at constant currencies, a sharp slowdown from nearly 100% growth in the previous quarter, but investors chose to focus on the core business instead.

Eyecare and medical technology, the company's traditional strength, grew more than 6%, showing resilient demand for ordinary glasses and lenses. The stock had roughly halved over the previous year, which made the relief rally larger.

The disclosure itself matters: by putting a number on wearables, the company is treating smart glasses as a real business line rather than an experiment. Watch whether growth re-accelerates during the holiday quarter.

items.title: Trump launches a $25 million program paying tipsters up to $30,000 for fraud reports
items.summary:
President Trump announced a $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program on Tuesday in the Oval Office. The Justice Department will run it, tips will be submitted through a government website, and individual awards will generally run from $10,000 to $30,000, with the president describing himself as the final arbiter of amounts.

The program sits inside Vice President JD Vance's anti-fraud task force, launched this year, which has looked at medical supply programs, food assistance and Affordable Care Act enrolments. Last month the task force said it would remove hundreds of thousands of exchange enrolments it judged ineligible or nonexistent.

Content creator Nick Shirley, whose viral video last year alleged fraud at Minnesota daycare centres — some of those allegations were later debunked by Minnesota outlets — was announced as an early $10,000 recipient at the event. The wider Minnesota social-services fraud prosecutions earlier led Governor Tim Walz to drop his bid for a third term.

Supporters call paid tips a practical way to surface fraud; critics will watch whether awards follow verified recoveries. The first test is what the Justice Department publishes about results.

items.title: Supreme Court keeps transgender prison care in place, rejecting the administration's emergency bid
items.summary:
The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the Trump administration must keep providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates in federal prisons while the underlying case continues. The justices denied the government's emergency request for a stay, without explanation, with Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito noted as willing to grant it.

The decision leaves in place a district judge's injunction from this summer barring the Bureau of Prisons from carrying out its policy of ending hormone therapy and related treatment. An appeals court had also refused to pause that injunction, and Solicitor General D. John Sauer then asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

The case, Kingdom v. Trump, covers about 1,000 inmates with a gender dysphoria diagnosis. The ACLU says more than 2,000 people in federal custody identify as transgender and about 800 have been prescribed hormone therapy, and notes the prison system has treated gender dysphoria since at least 1992.

This was an emergency order, not a final ruling on the policy's legality. Watch the lower-court case, which will decide the question on a full record.

items.title: Churches and synagogues win an appeals round in the fight over immigration raids at houses of worship
items.summary:
A federal appeals panel in Washington ruled 2-1 on Tuesday in favour of 27 religious organisations challenging immigration enforcement at houses of worship, reversing a lower court's refusal to consider a preliminary injunction and sending the case back for another look. It is a procedural win, not a final block on the policy.

At issue is the administration's January 2025 decision to rescind a long-standing policy limiting enforcement at sensitive locations such as churches, synagogues and schools — a policy first set in 2011 and expanded in 2021. The groups sued under the First Amendment, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the Administrative Procedure Act, citing falling attendance and fear among congregants.

Writing for the majority, Judge Florence Pan said the groups likely have standing and face likely, imminent harm, pointing to direct evidence the government intends to increase enforcement at sensitive locations. Judge Neomi Rao dissented, calling it speculative that restoring the earlier guidance would change enforcement on the ground.

The district court now reconsiders the injunction request under the panel's reasoning. Watch for that ruling, which could temporarily restore limits before any trial.

items.title: Man arrested in Pakistan in an alleged $126 million counterfeit U.S. postage scheme
items.source: Associated Press via New York Post
items.summary:
Pakistani authorities arrested Faheem Akram, 33, this week after a weeks-long search involving raids across the country, a senior official of Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency said. Akram, from Khanewal in Punjab province, has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida.

Prosecutors say he operated LabelsBank.com, an unauthorised site that sold more than 5.1 million counterfeit postage labels to more than 5,200 customers, typically for $2 each regardless of a package's weight, size or destination. The $126 million figure is the Postal Service's estimated loss in revenue and shipping costs, not the site's sales.

Investigators in Pakistan say the operation ran from August 2023 through September 2026 and used 16 bank accounts, including accounts held by relatives. The U.S. Attorney's Office statement in the case is dated Sept. 28.

It is not yet clear whether Akram will be extradited to the United States or tried in Pakistan. Watch for a first court appearance and any move against alleged partners or resellers.

items.title: Players' union demands a full investigation into how Jalen Hurts' blood clots were handled
items.summary:
The NFL players' union called Tuesday night for a full investigation into the medical care given to Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is likely out for the season with deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in his lungs. Hurts, 28, has been placed on injured reserve and is starting blood thinners.

The timeline is the heart of the dispute. A superficial clot in Hurts' calf was found on ultrasound on Oct. 10, the day before the Eagles played in London, and he was cleared to play that game. The lung clots were discovered after the team returned to Philadelphia. A joint statement from the team and his agent says he is clinically stable and expected to make a full recovery.

The union says it is not aware of any league investigation and that the NFL previously said it did not plan one. The league, meanwhile, has backed the Eagles' handling, and its chief medical officer dismissed concerns at a Tuesday press conference, with reporting that the league already concluded the care was appropriate.

Two institutions reaching opposite conclusions in public is exactly why the union wants a formal review. Watch whether the league opens one during its fall meetings this week.

items.title: FDA approves a first-of-its-kind hepatitis B drug that could let some patients stop treatment for good
items.summary:
The Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday approved GSK's Hibsago, known generically as bepirovirsen, for adults with chronic hepatitis B who do not have cirrhosis and who are already on antiviral therapy. It is the first approved antisense oligonucleotide for the disease, working by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to copy itself.

In two large Phase 3 trials, 19% of patients who received the drug achieved a functional cure 24 weeks after stopping all treatment, compared with none on placebo, and 24% met the criteria to stop their existing antiviral. That matters because today's standard treatments produce a lasting functional cure in only about 1% to 4% of patients and are often taken for life.

More than 250 million people worldwide live with chronic hepatitis B. The approval also included a companion diagnostic test from Roche to identify eligible patients, and the drug is already approved in Japan and under review in China and Europe.

GSK expects peak sales above $2.68 billion a year, but has not yet announced U.S. pricing. Watch for the price and for how quickly specialists adopt a treatment that asks patients to stop therapy they may have taken for years.

items.title: Columbus Dispatch endorses Amy Acton for governor over Vivek Ramaswamy
items.summary:
The Columbus Dispatch editorial board endorsed Democrat Amy Acton for governor on Wednesday, in an editorial written by Opinion Editor Amelia Robinson ahead of the Nov. 3 vote. The Akron Beacon Journal also endorsed Acton the same day.

Neither candidate has held elected office. Acton, from Youngstown, led Ohio's health department under Republican Governor Mike DeWine and would be the state's first woman and first Jewish governor. Ramaswamy, a Cincinnati-area biotech entrepreneur endorsed by President Trump, would be Ohio's first Hindu governor and first governor of colour.

The board backed Acton's platform on child care and pre-K, affordable housing, property-tax relief for older homeowners, protecting Medicaid — used by more than 3 million Ohioans — and school funding transparency. It also criticised her for refusing to debate Ramaswamy and for keeping reporters out of some events. The endorsement landed a day after a viral ad featuring Acton's estranged mother drew wide condemnation; a poll cited by the board found nearly 50% of Ohioans said Ramaswamy is doing more mudslinging, against 22.8% for Acton.

The race remains close despite Ramaswamy outspending Acton roughly three to one. Endorsements rarely decide races, but in a contest this tight, newspaper backing in Columbus and Akron gives Acton a useful closing argument.

items.title: Sherwin-Williams cuts Cleveland headquarters jobs in an operations review
items.summary:
Sherwin-Williams has cut about 40 positions at its Cleveland headquarters, the company reported this week, describing the reductions as part of an ongoing review of operations and resources. The cuts affected selected areas, and the company said they were not based on individual employees' performance.

The paint maker, founded in Cleveland in 1866, employs more than 6,000 people in Ohio, so the headquarters reduction is small in percentage terms. It still lands in a city where the company is one of the most visible corporate anchors, and where its long-planned headquarters project has been closely watched.

Investors' next focus is the company's third-quarter results, due before the market opens on Oct. 27, with a call on the outlook for the rest of the year. In the second quarter, Sherwin-Williams beat expectations with $6.79 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of $3.70 a share.

Watch the earnings call for whether management frames the cuts as a one-off adjustment or the start of a broader cost programme.

items.title: Cleveland's KeyCorp posts record revenue and a profit beat in the third quarter
items.summary:
Cleveland-based KeyCorp reported third-quarter net income of $537 million, or 51 cents a share, up 18.3% from a year earlier and ahead of the 46 cents analysts expected. Revenue reached a record $2.04 billion, up 8.4% from a year ago.

The growth was led by lending and fees. Net interest income rose 9.8% to $1.30 billion as margins widened, helped by lower deposit costs and commercial loan growth, while investment banking and debt placement fees jumped to $214 million. The commercial bank earned $516 million, and the consumer bank earned $211 million even as average consumer loans fell.

Credit quality improved at the same time: charge-offs fell to $89 million, the provision for future losses dropped to $61 million from $107 million, and nonperforming assets declined. The bank, with about $193 billion in assets, bought back $320 million of its own shares in the quarter.

Chief Executive Chris Gorman pointed to record pre-provision revenue and returns above 15%, with a goal of sustaining that level through 2027. For Cleveland, it is a reminder that one of its largest hometown employers is growing rather than shrinking.

items.title: Cleveland extends its data-center permit freeze into early 2027
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council has moved to extend the city's freeze on data-center permits until Jan. 29, 2027, or until new regulations take effect, whichever comes first. The pause had been set to expire on Oct. 20, and council records show the extension passed 11-1 under emergency procedures.

The freeze is broad: it halts review and issuance of use, building and zoning permits, occupancy certificates and other licences — including public utilities permits — for data centers anywhere in the city. Ward 13 Councilman Brian Kazy, who leads the effort through council's Data Center Working Group, held three town halls and says residents want clear rules on zoning, power-grid impact and water use before projects proceed.

Cleveland is not acting alone. Ohio had about 125 local data-center moratoriums as of September, including in North Royalton, Kent and Grove City, and Grafton approved a five-year pause. The state counts 80 data centers operating and 189 planned, most clustered around Columbus.

A statehouse committee is expected to shape a statewide bill, House Bill 646. Watch for Cleveland's permanent rules by the end of January — they will decide whether the city competes for these projects or keeps them out.

items.title: A Garfield statue that stood in Delaware for a century now calls Hiram, Ohio, home
items.summary:
A zinc statue of President James A. Garfield that watched over a Wilmington, Delaware, intersection since 1918 has been moved to Hiram, Ohio, the village where Garfield attended the college that now bears his era's name. Wilmington paid $21,500 for the move, split between the mayor's office and a council member's office.

The statue was sculpted in the 1890s and first stood on Delaware Avenue before spending more than a century at Concord Avenue and 23rd Street. In Hiram, about 30 miles southeast of Cleveland, it will sit in front of Village Hall. Garfield studied at what is now Hiram College from 1851 to 1854, and the village is about 20 miles from where he was born.

Wilmington's reasoning was simple: Garfield had no connection to that city. Council Member Shane Darby, who backed the move, praised Garfield as an abolitionist and civil-rights supporter and wants the vacated spot to become community and art space, with local artists being approached about its future.

Garfield, the 20th president, served from March 1881 until his assassination later that year. For Hiram, a town of fewer than 1,000 people, the statue is a tangible link to its most famous student.

items.title: New operator sought for Franklin County's largest homeless shelter as the YMCA steps away
items.summary:
The YMCA of Central Ohio will stop operating the Van Buren Emergency Shelter on June 30, 2027, the organisation and the Community Shelter Board announced jointly on Wednesday. The board will now seek proposals for multiple operators to run different parts of Franklin County's largest shelter.

Van Buren, a converted warehouse in South Franklinton that opened in 2014, houses about 520 people on an average night — adults and families, mostly in large rooms with bunk beds and mats, plus some private family rooms. On winter nights the count can pass 650. The facility has faced long-running criticism over cleanliness and safety, though YMCA chief Tony Collins said the exit is a strategic shift toward prevention and long-term housing stability, not a reaction to that criticism.

Both organisations promised no gap in service during the transition, and the YMCA will keep providing case management to help people move from shelter into stable housing. Shelter Board chief Shannon Isom tied the shelter's continuing need to Columbus's shortage of deeply affordable housing.

The board's longer direction is away from large congregate shelters altogether — but it acknowledges emergency beds still fill a nightly gap for hundreds of people. Watch the operator search for whether a new model emerges.

baby.tip: Hospital-bag week: pack two bags — one for labor and delivery (documents, chargers, snacks for Mike, toiletries, a going-home outfit for Kelly) and one for postpartum and baby (two outfit sizes, since newborn vs 0–3 month fit is a coin toss). Leave them by the door or in the MDX so a midnight departure is grab-and-go. Anything clinical about what to bring for recovery — ask your OB at the next visit.
baby.fact: Newborns arrive with a stomach about the size of a cherry — roughly a teaspoon of milk per feed on day one — which is why tiny, frequent feeds are completely normal at first. By about a week old it has grown to roughly the size of an egg.
